incoming.explanation: Reasons from the established colonial occupation fact (John a tailor by trade), whose canonical home is g13-colonial-braintree-community.
The orientation rests on the colonial occupation fact - that John was a tailor - whose canonical home is the Braintree-community unit.
The occupation finding (a tailor by trade) is one strand of the shared matching-criteria profile.

outgoing.explanation: The 12 February 1661/2 deed styling 'John Gurney, tailor' is the direct documentary evidence of the trade.
The livestock-and-husbandry profile of the estate (the material-life husbandry finding) is the farming economy that overtook the trade in practice.
The 1663 inventory's absence of any tailoring tool (the material-life negative) qualifies how central the needle remained to his late-life economy.

finding.shortLabel: Occupation: a tailor by trade, a husbandman by economy

sources.alignmentNote: Sprague, Genealogies of the Families of Braintree, p. 695, John Gurney entry — compiled derivative genealogy recording John as a tailor of Braintree; corroborates the primary 1661/2 deed, not independent primary evidence.

finding.statement: John Gurney's trade was tailoring — he is styled 'John Gurney, tailor' in his own 12 February 1661/2 Braintree deed, and Sprague's compiled Braintree genealogy likewise enters him as a tailor — but the working economy of his last years was a husbandman's: his March 1663 estate inventory held no tool of the tailoring trade and its value lay in livestock, plough-gear, and grain. His occupation is best read as a trained trade overtaken in practice by mixed farming: a tailor by name, a husbandman by the measure of his goods.
